What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

📅 11 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and key meditation about masculinity.
  • According to recent reports, will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity?
  • I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and key meditation about masculinity.

According to recent reports, will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he remarked to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”.

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he notes, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”.

It has been revealed that finally, he indicates that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”.

In a recent development, in 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

It has been revealed that danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

13 Easy Holiday Mocktail Recipes For Entertaining Guests (Or Just Yourself)

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I love a good drink — whether it’s a canned cocktail or a jam jargarita, sign me up.
  • Industry observers note that since they make nonalcoholic and boozy ginger beer, ginger beer-based recipes are some of the easiest to make into mocktails on the fly.
  • I love it when a mocktail recipe makes up for its lack of booze with an overabundance of fun in another form.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes you just need a special bevvie.

I love a good drink — whether it’s a canned cocktail or a jam jargarita, sign me up. But even I sometimes fall back on a good old mocktail, whether I just can’t handle a red wine hangover tomorrow or because I’m hosting and there needs to be an NA option. These easy holiday mocktail recipes are perfect for those moments when you need to whip up a big batch of something festive to drink that’s safe for the whole family. Some are nonalcoholic versions of cocktails you know and love, while others are just fun, festive drinks to serve in place of something spiked.

Industry observers note that since they make nonalcoholic and boozy ginger beer, ginger beer-based recipes are some of the easiest to make into mocktails on the fly. All The Healthy Things’ bevvie is bubbly, fruity, and slightly herby — and it looks so stinking cute with “frosted” cranberries on top.

I love it when a mocktail recipe makes up for its lack of booze with an overabundance of fun in another form. In Averie Cooks’ recipe for caramel apple cider, it’s a homemade caramel sauce all around the rim — I’m in. You could totally use store-bought sauce to save time, but if you have to simmer the cider anyway, it might be fun to try.

If you’re making drinks for guests who don’t mind something super sweet (kids will lose it for this stuff), you’ve got to make Princess Pinky Girl’s Grinch punch. It’s a bright green blend of sherbet, green Hawaiian Punch, Sprite, and juice, so it will hurt many people’s teeth. But sweet-toothed friends, this one’s for you.

Recent findings suggest that holiday party snuck up on you and you’re in charge of drinks? Whip up this super easy holiday punch from Damn Delicious. All you have to do is mix together some ginger ale, pineapple juice, and cranberry juice, and load it up with some fresh fruits before serving.

Want a more decadent drink for a movie marathon at home? You have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s apple cider float recipe. It’s basically like a milkshake and apple cider had a baby and then dressed it up in warm, seasonal spices.

Recent findings suggest that think about how happy you’d be if you showed up at a holiday party and there was a self-serve vat of hot chocolate waiting for you. Well, be the change you wish to see in the world with Princess Pinky Girl’s Crockpot peppermint hot chocolate. While technically not a mocktail in that it’s not imitating a cocktail, a gussied-up take on hot chocolate still feels really festive and exciting to try.

This apple cider shrub mocktail from Budget Bytes is the drink if you like a not-so-sweet mocktail that tastes almost like it could be boozy. The drink has a few steps that’ll make you look like a professional bartender, but it’s easy enough that even a first-timer around a cocktail shaker can pull it off. Bonus points: They’re also incredibly cheap to make.

In a recent development, dirty soda, as a drink category, got plenty of attention this year thanks to the cast of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. So if you need a fun NA drink to serve your reality TV-loving friends, what could be better? Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe will teach you how to get the perfect balance of flavors if it’s your first time wading into dirty soda territory.

Haute & Healthy Living’s pomegranate sparkler looks like the perfect thing to swirl around in one hand while you make a cozy dinner. It still feels special — when else do most of us spring for pomegranate juice? — and has seasonal touches that give you all the festive feels of a cocktail.

It has been revealed that our Love Language Is Food’s spiced cider mocktail proves that as long as you have a fancy glass and a sugar-and-spice rim, you can make your beverage feel celebratory. These just look aggressively clink-able.

Want to make a substantial batch of punch for the party? Haute & Healthy Living’s recipe blends apple juice, orange concentrate, and cranberry cocktail, plus a few extra touches to bring it to life. It’s so easy to make, you can refill the bowl in a few minutes mid-party.

If you just can’t with all the sweet this and spiced that, Simply LaKita’s blackberry thyme mocktail is perfect for you. It’s simple, fizzy, and way less dessert-in-a-glass-inspired that many winter mocktails tend to be.

Which mocktails are you adding to your hosting repertoire this year?

#9454. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

📅 03 Jan 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2893 w)

8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

📅 03 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moms

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com.
  • It has been revealed that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years.
  • She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

It has been revealed that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite indicates for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

According to recent reports, A little online searching will promptly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

In a recent development, for many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

According to recent reports, when it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to strategy. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

Sources indicate that of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a substantial decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

According to recent reports, what are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

It has been revealed that weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

According to recent reports, the umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only glitch they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

According to recent reports, when you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

In a recent development, the charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

Industry observers note that the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

Recent findings suggest that the struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

In a recent development, these wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

According to recent reports, my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

Industry observers note that the fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Industry observers note that take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that one of the most painful things about being an adult child is realizing that your parents may never become the people you keep hoping they will be.
  • Recent findings suggest that you tell her something hurt you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why your boomer parents keep defending instead of hearing you, and how to break the stalemate.

It has been revealed that one of the most painful things about being an adult child is realizing that your parents may never become the people you keep hoping they will be. You can be 38, 48, or 58 years old, with a career, children, a mortgage, and a fairly sophisticated understanding of your own emotional life, and still find yourself on the phone with your mother feeling 12 years old.

Recent findings suggest that you tell her something hurt you. She tells you that you are too sensitive. You try to explain why the comment landed badly. She reminds you that she did the best she could. By the end of the conversation, you're not sure whether you're asking for an apology, trying to be understood, or hoping (once again) that this time she will respond differently.

In my work with adult children navigating conflict with their boomer parents, I see a recurring pattern: The adult child experiences a parent's rigidity, defensiveness, or denial as evidence that the parent doesn't care.

In a recent development, sometimes that interpretation is accurate. There are parents who are cruel, manipulative, dismissive, or unwilling to take responsibility. But often, what looks like malice is also a generational mismatch in how people understand emotional responsibility, conflict, and attachment.

Many boomers were raised in families where children were expected to adapt to adults, not the other way around. Feelings were often treated as private matters, discipline was framed as character-building, and parents were not necessarily expected to explain themselves or repair a rupture after an argument. For some, love was expressed through provision, sacrifice, and showing up materially. The idea that a parent should validate a child's emotional experience — even when the parent remembers the event differently — can feel foreign, or even accusatory.

In a recent development, that history can help explain why a parent responds to “That hurt me” with “Well, I did my best,” or to “I need you to listen” with a list of everything they have done for you. The adult child is asking for emotional recognition in the present. The parent hears a verdict on their entire history as a mother or father. One person is trying to talk about impact; the other is defending intent. They are having two different conversations, and both leave feeling unseen.

Sources indicate that this is the pattern I want adult children to understand... not because it excuses harmful behavior, but because it can change what you do next.

If you interpret every defensive response as proof that your parent has no love for you, you may keep escalating the argument in search of a kind of recognition they are not currently able to offer.

In a recent development, you may explain more, provide more examples, produce more evidence, and try increasingly precise language. Meanwhile, your parent may become more entrenched, because each fresh explanation feels like another charge they have to defend against.

According to recent reports, A reframe can help: instead of asking, “Why won't my parent admit they hurt me?” try asking, “What kind of response is this person actually capable of giving me?” That is not the same as accepting the response or deciding it is enough. It is an assessment of reality. You can want your parent to understand you and also recognize that they may not have the emotional vocabulary, flexibility, or willingness to do so.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes a more effective conversation begins with a smaller, more concrete request. Rather than asking a parent to acknowledge an entire pattern of emotional neglect, you might say, “When I tell you something is hard, I need you to listen before you tell me what I should have done.” Rather than trying to settle the history of your relationship over dinner, you might say, “I'm not asking you to agree with my memory. I'm asking you not to tell me I'm making it up.”.

The goal is not to shrink your needs to make them palatable. It is to make the request clear enough that you can see whether your parent is willing to meet it.

There is also a difference between understanding a parent's limitations and organizing your life around them. If a parent repeatedly dismisses your feelings, violates boundaries, or uses guilt to control you, you are allowed to limit what you share, shorten visits, decline certain conversations, or take space.

Sources indicate that A generational explanation is not a hall pass. It can offer context, but it does not erase impact or require you to keep making yourself available for the same injury.

Recent findings suggest that I also encourage adult children to notice when they are still approaching a parent as though the right argument will finally produce the childhood experience they missed. This is deeply human. We want our parents to see us, to be curious about us, to take responsibility when they hurt us. But sometimes the work is grieving the parent we needed while deciding what kind of relationship is possible with the parent we actually have.

It has been revealed that that grief can coexist with affection. You can understand that your mother was doing what she knew how to do and still wish she had done something different. You can appreciate what your father provided and still name what was missing. You can have compassion for the conditions that shaped your parents without making those conditions your responsibility to repair.

The most useful question may not be whether your parents are bad people or whether you are asking too much. It may be whether the relationship you have today can hold the kind of honesty you want to bring to it. If it can, try a smaller, clearer conversation. If it cannot, boundaries may be more productive than another attempt to persuade.

Growing up doesn't always mean finally getting your parents to understand you. Sometimes it means learning to understand the limits of the relationship... and deciding, with care and without self-abandonment, what you want to do with that knowledge.

  • Recent findings suggest that for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

In a Newly introduced York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”.

Recent findings suggest that for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

Recent findings suggest that in Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

Recent findings suggest that it’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a new approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, big picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

According to recent reports, dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

But we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

Sources indicate that for example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

Sources indicate that you talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

Yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

Industry observers note that it is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

You're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

In a recent development, I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

According to recent reports, and so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

So what role should parents take?

In a recent development, if you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

In a recent development, I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

The crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that indicates that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

Sources indicate that and the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

Industry observers note that what happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

So one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically notes that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

According to recent reports, so what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Sources indicate that let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

In a recent development, right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

Recent findings suggest that and the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

In a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

You say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

That's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

One thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the significant feelings in a household? How do you let problems not get carried away?

So one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

The other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

Industry observers note that for example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

It has been revealed that anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter said to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?".

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I remarked, "Okay, do you like it?".

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

According to recent reports, exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence is everywhere now. It has become part of most Americans’ work and personal lives at an unprecedented pace, popping up in our inboxes and social media apps even when we haven’t opted into a chatbot ourselves. Examples of the harm have rolled in, from staggering numbers of deepfake nudes being created of children to teens who turn to AI for advice during a mental health crisis. But in New York, new legislation will try to rein in the technology and the risks it poses to minors.

The new law, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, prohibits companies with AI chatbots “from offering unsafe features to minors, including chatbots that pretend to be human, build emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage in sexually explicit conversations.” Companies would have to block these features on the accounts of anyone under 18, or any user whose age has not been verified. The law requires chatbot providers to verify consumers through multiple age assurance methods.

Sources indicate that once verified, that age information must be deleted. It was signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 28, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that according to Gov. Hochul’s website, the legislation prohibits AI chatbots from, among other things:.

Violations of the newly introduced law could result in fines of up to $25,000 per infraction. The attorney general will publish a new website where New Yorkers can file complaints. New York’s new law is an attempt to curtail the behaviors that are most harmful to kids, experts say.

The story of Adam Raine — a teenager who died by suicide, and whose conversations with ChatGPT exposed that it offered to write his suicide note for him — is one example of why humanizing chatbot behaviors like these are targeted by this law. Surveys have shown kids ages 11 to 16 can’t really articulate what AI is, and many ascribe human-like consciousness and emotions to chatbots.

Recent findings suggest that “Children are developing these relationships because they are vulnerable to do so. It’s not enough for companies to just put in guardrails for something that happens after the fact. What they’re asking companies to do is to understand the risks and build according to what we believe those risks are,” claims Dona Fraser, SVP of Privacy Initiatives at BBB National Programs, an independent industry accountability organization. “We need to be able to distinguish between the beneficial uses of AI and the design features that create these unnecessary risks.”.

According to a 2026 Common Sense Media report, nearly 9 in 10 kids ages 9 to 17 (86%) interact with AI, including about one in four who use it on a daily basis. More than half of kids (57%) who use AI said they’ve used it to get information about their health or body; separate studies have found that AI gives misleading or inaccurate health information to people 50% of the time. Half of the respondents have asked AI for advice on decisions about their future or goals, while 37% have used chatbots to discuss their feelings or personal problems.

As always, legislation lumbers along while technology speeds ahead unchecked. Until the laws catch up to AI, parents can feel alone in the fight to protect their kids. Fraser indicates this law on its own is not enough to protect them either.

“Legislation alone cannot guarantee safety. Companies have got to do their part, and there has got to be accountability,” she claims. “The Meta settlements are a great example of what industry self-regulation looks like. It doesn’t work. There’s got to be third-party independent accountability because companies, for all sorts of reasons, can’t always take five steps back to see what it is that they’re doing. Sometimes they can't see the risks that are right in front of them. So I do think that the law is a step in the right direction. We need these types of laws, but we also need the companies to do their part.”.

Sources indicate that as New York readies to enforce its new youth AI protections, just this week Google, Meta, and TikTok filed a lawsuit against the state of California, challenging its legislation prohibiting addictive social media features on children’s accounts. The law bans the platforms from offering “psychologically exploitative features” to minors, including autoplay videos, endless scroll, and personalized recommendations that contribute to “compulsive use.” The companies argue the government is trying to impose its judgment over parents'.

The “Saved By The Bell” alum has come full circle and is now playing a principal and mom.

Sources indicate that tiffani Amber Thiessen’s face is burned into the brains of every elder Millennial who watched countless Saved by the Bell episodes and dreamed of dressing exactly like Kelly Kapowski. Of course, we’ve all left the 1900s behind and have grown into adults — parents and women with careers.

Like the rest of us, the 52-year-old mom of two kids — Harper, 16, and Holt, 11 — has left high school in the rear view mirror, but her career continues to flourish. And she’s still in the classroom, in a way: Coven Academy, the witchy dark academia series in which she stars as the principal of Crescent Veil Academy, just got renewed for a second season.

You can also find her on Instagram, where her account is a delightful mix of food, fashion, humor, nostalgia, and life as a woman who is finding power and peace as she enters her 50s.

It has been revealed that recently, Thiessen partnered with Always on its “Period Talks Don’t Have to Be Scary” campaign, which addresses what is often a real hurdle for parents: talking about periods with their kids. Research has found that 43% of moms struggle to start the first-period talk because they feel unprepared. So Thiessen wants to share her own experiences while offering practical advice to parents who want to open and informative with their tweens and teens... even if can be awkward at times.

She recently sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about periods, parenting, her new show, and her family’s holiday traditions.

Industry observers note that scary Mommy: Gen Z and Millennial moms have done a lot to break period stigma with our kids. How have you done that with your kids?

It has been revealed that tiffani Amber Thiessen: I think the generation I grew up in didn’t talk about these things. Now kids are much more open, and I have a very open relationship with both my children. It never fully takes away the scariness of intimate talks, whether it’s periods, the body, or growing up. But I think parents who understand that it isn’t one substantial, intimidating conversation, but many small, casual talks, can take the edge off.

Partnering with Always has been lovely because they’re trying to prepare parents with what to do and how to have that first conversation. Being prepared gives you the confidence.

SM: I found that I was a lot more scared than my daughter was. Did you feel that?

Sources indicate that TAT: Most parents feel that way. You don’t realize until afterward that it really isn’t that scary. I found it to be a bonding moment. I’d tell my kids that over half the population menstruates, so it’s not a big deal. Keeping it casual and a little funny helps. Building that competence between parent and child is what lets your daughter take it on, and it’s a badge of honor.

SM: I love asking this: What’s your best piece of parenting advice?

TAT: It goes back to having an open conversation about anything. When I became a parent, I wanted to be open to receiving anything my kids share, whether it’s hard or difficult. I wanted them to feel comfortable and know I would never judge. We’ve all been in crazy places, and my kids are super open with me, about the fun stuff and the stuff that isn’t so fun. Keeping that conversation free of judgment is probably the most important thing in parenting.

SM: Have you ever wanted to judge, though?

It has been revealed that TAT: I can secretly judge, is that okay? [laughs].

According to recent reports, TAT: Most of the things my kids tell me I’ve either witnessed, been through, or know someone who has. It’s really not that crazy.

SM: Let’s switch gears to Coven Academy. And you just got renewed for Season 2?

Industry observers note that TAT: Monday! We had high hopes and wanted to find an audience that saw the specialness of the show, and I think we did. It’s done very well on Disney+ and Hulu, so we’re over the moon to do it all over again.

Recent findings suggest that SM: There are so few shows made for this demographic: tweens, mostly girls. It’s so good to have something that speaks to kids in that space.

TAT: The witch aspect is having a moment on social media, but it’s not really about spells and potions. It’s about found family, sisterhood, and having each other’s backs. I have a teenage daughter, and she has a wonderful group of girls she can count on. Everybody should have that, especially women.

SM: How has it been going from being a student on a hugely popular show to a headmistress on set with the younger generation?

Sources indicate that TAT: It feels natural. I have kids of my own now. The last few shows I’ve been fortunate to do have had younger casts, and I really enjoy working with young adults. I may give them advice, but I get a lot from them, too. We did a lot of night shoots, and I’d see these kids at 3 a.m. doing their TikToks while I was struggling. Their energy kept me going through those nights.

In a recent development, SM: The holidays are coming up. Do you have any family traditions you want to share?

In a recent development, TAT: We’re very traditional in that it’s all about family. We do Christmas morning and Christmas Eve dinner. For the last 15 or 16 years, we’ve alternated between my husband’s family in Texas and ours. This year it’s our turn to go to Texas. We leave the day after Christmas and spend the week and Fresh Year’s with my in-laws. All the cousins are together, and we look forward to it every year.

SM: What have you been cooking lately, or what are you planning for the holidays?

Industry observers note that TAT: My kids like the traditions. Thanksgiving is classic turkey and stuffing, plus my mom’s famous cream cheese pie. For Christmas we usually do enchiladas, which I’ll probably make again this year. We usually switch it up for Christmas because everybody’s over turkey.

SM: Dennis Haskins recently passed away. He was your principal on Saved by the Bell, and now you’re playing a principal. Do you have any remembrances to share?

TAT: I have so many. He was our solid one; our anchor. I know it was probably hard for him, being the only adult on a kids’ show. He handled it with such grace and gave us a safe place. He was part of us, and he could be young, but he was still a strong personality. He always made us feel protected, and he’s very much missed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.
  • Recent findings suggest that two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth.
  • The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Recent findings suggest that two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

In a recent development, the second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

In a recent development, both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

“Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Recent findings suggest that parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

According to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

According to recent reports, A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

#9443. It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

📅 02 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time.
  • It has been revealed that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing.
  • Industry observers note that I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time. There’s another way.

It has been revealed that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing. That’s my cynical summary of so many experts who study such things. When it comes to screen science, I’ve attended the lectures, seen the documentaries, read the books, gone to parent meetups, and flipped through the studies. I’ve been through it personally with my high schooler — hooked, caught in dangerous situations, experiencing mental health crises thanks to the online world. My third-grader is phone-free and blissfully unaware (well, he loves Tears of the Kingdom, but that seems downright educational these days), but I still work so hard to get ahead of it.

Industry observers note that I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount. Hell, I’ve helped to start and run a PTA committee whose purpose is to look critically at screen time and help foster independence in kids. There’s a lot of movement. And yet, it feels like parents are American revolutionaries in 1773. We’re dumping tea into the harbor and an impossibly well-funded army is coming to get us.

This past week I took the fight overseas. I had the pleasure of talking with Kaitlyn Regehr, Ph.D., a researcher and professor of digital humanities at University College London and author of Smartphone Nation, out now. The tagline of the book is spot on: “Building Digital Boundaries When Offline Isn't an Option.” It’s a go-to book that’s informative, but not overly complex, exhaustive, but surprisingly short and to the point, and lacking in the shame that so many screen time books put on parents. I can't recommend it enough.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

According to recent reports, I'd love to start with the idea of digital pyramids, if that's OK. Like the food pyramid, it can be a really helpful guide to how we and our kids should consume media. Would you mind just walking us through that idea?

Recent findings suggest that I think the idea of healthy eating is something we understand. The food pyramid, similar to the digital diet pyramid, is weighted with the good nutritious things at the bottom and the not-so-good things, the things that we want to limit, at the top. We might not always choose to follow it. We might sometimes eat a tub of ice cream, but we are aware that we are making that choice. I think what the digital diet pyramid does is it allows people and parents, most particularly, to think about the choices that they are constantly making every time they open a screen. Generally, what we want to do if we want a healthy relationship to screens is we want to be thinking about active, educational, informative, healthy socialization as forming the base of that pyramid. And then farther up the top are things like passive consumption, doom scrolling, short-form, low-quality content that we want to mitigate or moderate to a certain degree.

In the digital pyramid, where do you place movies and cinematic video games? I think, these days, a kid who can watch a full movie or pay attention to hours of plot in one of those cinematic video games kind of has a leg up. Do you agree?

Right. So you are talking about long-form content versus short-form content and how that relates to the development of attention spans and the ability to follow full narratives through. Absolutely, not all screen time is created equal. What we want to be doing, where possible, is, of course, running around outside is normally better, but if you are going to use screens, we want that screen time to ideally be long-form engagement, like good quality movies, where possible, interactive engagement and collective viewing.

Recent findings suggest that so particularly with young children, ideally, you are sitting there with them watching a Julie Andrews movie talking about the content, using it as a springboard for their discussion. If it takes place during World War II, maybe that is a discussion point for you to talk a little bit about history and use the viewing as a jumping-off point for education and for communication. That's where we really want to be with screen consumption, if we are going to be using those screens. Generally, the bigger the screen and the longer the content, the better.

So Mary Poppins over Roblox, that's my takeaway from this.

I appreciate how Smartphone Nation repeats the idea that screens aren't all bad and that the concept of “screen time” can shame parents for turning to screens ever. I think your book is a nice counterpoint to The Anxious Generation’s Jonathan Haidt, which primarily argues that taking away phones and getting kids outside is the answer. You note that being digitally native isn't all bad. So my question for you is, if screen time limits aren't the answer, where should we start?

First, let's talk about where screen time comes from as a concept. Screen time, that guidance came out of some pretty good physical health research, mostly around childhood obesity and childhood diabetes from about 15 years ago. What that research noted was, "If kids are sedentary, if they are sitting in front of screens all the time, they aren't moving around, that's bad for their physical health." That is still true. And Jonathan Haidt's argument around that is true. If you are in front of screens, you're not moving around, and that's not good for your physical health and aspects of your mental health, and I absolutely agree with that. But that guidance really just captured the quantity of the screen consumption, and not the quality of the screen consumption. So that guidance is limiting in that it doesn't address the mental health implications of what kids might be consuming on screens.

It has been revealed that as we discussed previously, it's a very different scenario to have a kid watching with their parents Mary Poppins than for them to be alone in their bedroom with headphones on, scrolling through an algorithmically-driven feed. That is qualitatively a very different experience. The sad thing is that a Pew research study has recently pointed out that 89% of kids from the age of 5 are on YouTube now, an algorithmically driven, largely unregulated platform, and I think it's about 81% from the age of 3. Now, most of the discussions that we have at the moment around algorithms, around social media, completely leave out those younger years, and they tend to leave YouTube out of that discussion. But really for a lot of us, well-meaning parents, without realizing it, we're actually grooming our kids into these algorithmically-driven short-form, often low-quality content, from a really early age. So what we need to get to grips of is that not all screen time is equal and that we're actually needing to make an active choice.

Fortunately, there are many more choices available to us as parents than our parents had to make. That's not to say that we weren't plopped in front of screens to watch hours of content with bad-quality TV dinners (we were), but these were different screens and it was different content. Those were largely regulated spaces, often programmed by children's commissioners who were experts in programming children's content that had a diversity of content. You weren't watching 10 episodes of Bluey in a row. Those regulated spaces that a lot of good advocacy went into in order to develop, if we think of the development of children's programming on PBS, unfortunately, a lot of that good work has been thrown out the window because those kids are not on those spaces anymore, they're on YouTube, and that is a great tragedy.

Industry observers note that I think it's really vital as parents that we remind ourselves that we are making choices. But because we are making choices, we can make different choices and we can make empowered decisions about the types of screens and the types of digital spaces we want our kids to inhabit. There's great empowerment in that I think.

You just mentioned how even Bluey could be problematic, which I've actually never thought about. It is a really good point. If you give the kid the control or you let it auto-rotate and do eight in a row, Bluey is a completely different experience. Whereas, usually, it's the safest possible space for parents with young kids.

I'm not saying that Bluey is problematic. It's not problematic. What is problematic is allowing a binge watching of an entire season. We actually should be having diversity of content. There are great things about curated spaces, and there are great things about children's programming that has carefully thought through what comes after what and that there's some kind of host that comes in and makes sense of things for kids. Terrestrial TV is a very different experience. When I speak to my kids who are still very little about healthy screen consumption, I talk about terrestrial TV. I talk about algorithms and the fact that algorithms make our choices for us. It's important that we're active in our decision-making and that there are experts and, in the post-truth world, it's worth acknowledging, that there are some people that curate viewing experiences and these are regulated spaces. That means that that's a different experience so that there are healthy forms of screen consumption and less healthy forms of screen consumption.

Sources indicate that now, that is not to say that running around outside is still a much better thing to do. Of course, it is. But if you are going to use a screen, it's good to be much more intentional about how you do it.

If I can move to a slightly older audience. I have a teen myself, so I think about this all the time. How do I stop my kid from getting red-pilled?

It has been revealed that when we talk about online extremism or the echo chambers that our kids or our uncles or ourselves might be in, I think it's really vital to take a step back and think about the technological processes at play. The reason that young boys are often fed online misogyny or more extreme content is because it is more attention-grabbing. The reason that girls are fed body dysmorphic content and self-harm is because it's more attention-grabbing. The financial structures of social media are an attention economy. The whole system is set up to hold our attention as long as possible and, in fact, hold our attention a little longer each time. Unfortunately, that often means that hate, harm, and disinformation are often algorithmically prioritized because they are more attention-grabbing, because disinformation is often more attention-grabbing than truth.

Sources indicate that one of the best things we can do, and we absolutely should be doing this with teenagers, is talking about that concept, talking about the attention economy, talking about the way in which we are manipulated through social media, and our usage and our behaviors online are collected in order to manipulate us, just to hold us a little bit longer. If you talk to kids about this idea, even from early teenage years, they don't like it. They don't like the idea of being emotionally manipulated and controlled. One thing that I talk about with any type of echo chamber is instead of fighting or debating your teenager or uncle at Thanksgiving dinner around the specificity of the issue, around the granular detail. It's better to take a step back, collectivize, and talk about the ways in which these technological and corporate structures are feeding them this content and pushing them potentially down a narrower and narrower path.

And then it becomes you together against those structures, and that becomes a very powerful thing. One, you are equipping your young person with tools to be empowered digital citizens, and, two, it's something you're in together because you yourself are not immune to it and you are probably being fed something different, but it may be something that makes you feel bad.

Recent findings suggest that this one's for parents of neurodivergent kids. It seems that we are getting pulled in two directions. On one hand, social media is more dangerous. One study you cited noted that the likelihood of seeing self-harm content is, tell me if I'm getting this right, 40% greater for those with mental health difficulties, 31% greater for kids with autism. On the other hand, you also write that evidence suggests that screens can provide predictability and a sense of belonging within like-minded communities and can be instrumental in helping neurodiverse kids manage anxiety. Can you please walk us through this?

Sources indicate that I think this goes back to this idea of quality consumption and the choices that we make around our screens. That work around social media-fed harm or algorithmically-prioritized harm and the way in which neurodiverse kids are disproportionately targeted is immensely problematic, and, if you have a neurodiverse child, something you should be aware of. That is not unique to neurodiverse children. Social media is very, very good at predicting our behaviors, but also at knowing our vulnerabilities because it is through those vulnerabilities that it can point out [what we] lack and we are more susceptible to buying things if we feel a lack. That fits into this business model. The work that has been done around the way in which screens can support neurodiversity tends to be around ways in which screens can be used to calm kids, ways in which different learning applications can support neurodiverse kids, and that there are ways in which differently abled kids might find community through the internet. That remains true and those are good things, but of course we're almost talking about different usages of screens. That stuff is not happening on TikTok in the same way. It just really isn't.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of the discussions that we used to have around the beauty of social media a decade ago and the way it gave platforms for speaking voice and finding community has shifted as the technology has become more and more sophisticated and more and more manipulative. When we talk about that good stuff, we really need to be careful about how we're carving out those spaces, what screens we're using to do them, and where those screens are being used.

In another sense, keep kids away from the algorithms.

Industry observers note that yeah. For younger teenagers, I tend to find that algorithmically driven content is more and more problematic. As these systems become more and more sophisticated, they will be able to hold our kids' eyeballs longer and longer and longer, and we have to push back against that.

Industry observers note that hear, hear.
